## During my first professional decade

- Reading and studying papers introducing some data analysis method.
- What do all those formulas and equations mean?
- Is there code to apply those tools?
- Can I write code to implement those methods?
- Are authors willing to share some of their data/results with me?
- Can I obtain the same results?
- Can/Should I package my code?
- Can/Should I share my packages?
- Can/Should I write tutorials for my packages?


## During my first professional decade

- Statistical consulting for some client.
- What problem(s) or goal(s) do they have?
- What questions are they trying to answer?
    + Is it something I know how to approach/address?
- What data do they have (if any)?
- How should I carry out the analysis?
- What products should I deliver?

- What things should I avoid doing?
- What things should I never do again?

# A Few Horror Stories 😱


## 1. Saving Multiple Versions of a File

. . .

A student builds an amazing regression model at 2:00 AM. Exhausted, they save 
the code as `model_final.py`. 

. . .

The next morning, they realize they missed an outlier, 
tweak the file, and save it as `model_final_v2.py`. 

. . .

Two weeks later, their professor 
asks for a minor adjustment. They end up with `model_final_revised_PROFCORRECTED.py`. 

. . .

:::poll
When looking back at the folder a month later, they have no idea which 
file generated the actual metrics in their final presentation slide deck.
:::


## 2. Hardcoding Absolute Paths

. . .

Alex writes a brilliant data cleaning script on his Windows laptop.

. . .

He uploads it to a shared folder so his lab partner, Chloe, can run it on her MacBook. 

. . .

The second Chloe hits execute, the terminal crashes with a fatal 
[_File Not Found Error_]{.hilit}. 

. . .

:::poll
The script failed instantly because Chloe's computer doesn't have a user named 
"Alex," and Mac operating systems don't even use a `C:/` drive design. 
:::


## 3. Polluting the Global Environment

. . .

Maria installs **Pandas version 1.5** globally on her laptop to run a machine learning 
project for a class. 

. . .

Next semester, she takes an advanced statistics class that requires a new 
feature only found in **Pandas version 2.2**. She runs a global upgrade command. 

. . .

:::poll
When she tries to re-run her old machine learning code for her portfolio, 
it completely crashes with syntax errors.
:::


## 4. Silent Corruptions

. . .

David notices that a few rows in his sensor log dataset contain a typo: 
`"N/A"` instead of blank spaces. 

. . .

He opens the raw file in Microsoft Excel, uses **"Find and Replace"** 
to clean them up, hits save, and closes the window. 

. . .

What he doesn't realize is that Excel silently reformatted his entire 
[Date]{.mdlit} column from standard `YYYY-MM-DD` strings into a localized 
format like `MM/DD/YY`, and dropped the leading zeros on all his zip codes. 

. . .

:::poll
His Python analysis script now breaks completely because 
the data was fundamentally altered by a silent software default.
:::


## 5. Out-of-Order Executions

. . .

Sam is actively prototyping a data chart:

- He runs cell 1 to load data, 
- skips down to cell 10 to drop missing values,
- runs cell 4 to alter a variable, 
- and then jumps back to cell 2 to plot the results. 

. . .

The graph looks perfect. He saves the notebook and emails it 
to his professor. 

. . .

The professor opens the file, hits **"Run All Cells"** from top to bottom, 
and gets an entirely different chart with a broken trendline. 

. . .

:::poll
The perfect result only existed because of the chaotic, 
invisible memory sequence trapped inside Sam's live session.
:::


## 6. Dangers of Copy-Pasting

. . .

Elena computes a critical p-value for her research paper: `0.00412`. 
She opens her jupyter notebook, and types it in. 

. . .

Later that week, she realizes her input data had duplicated rows, 
so she runs the script again. The new correct p-value changes to `0.0412`. 

. . .

Because the report is a completely detached text file, she forgets to update 
the document manually. 

. . .

:::poll
She accidentally publishes a report with a massive typo that completely flips 
the statistical significance of her research.
:::


## 7. Unrepeatable Breakthroughs

. . .

A student builds a fraud-detection model that achieves an impressive 
95% accuracy score.

. . . 

Excitedly, she calls her supervisor over to show them the breakthrough. 
She hits execution again to demonstrate the live pipeline. 

. . .

The accuracy drops to 89%. She runs it a third time, and it jumps to 92%. 

. . .

:::poll
Because she forgot to hardcode a random seed marker (`numpy.random.seed(42)`), 
the dataset splits randomly on every execution, rendering her breakthrough 
metrics entirely un-reproducible.
:::


## 8. The Interactive GUI Trap

. . .

Kevin uses a graphical enterprise software program to clean a dataset, 
clicking visual buttons to remove columns, drop null rows, and filter outliers. 

. . .

He exports a beautiful chart for a corporate presentation. 

. . .

Six months later, a regulatory compliance officer demands an audit trail 
detailing exactly why certain outlier rows were dropped from the dataset. 

. . .

:::poll
Because Kevin handled the entire process through manual mouse clicks inside
a black-box GUI rather than writing a programmatic script, he has no way to 
prove or replicate his step-by-step logic, putting the validity of the 
entire project at risk.
:::


## 9. The Single-Commit Mega-Upload

. . .

Ryan works diligently on an assignment for three weeks without committing 
a single line of code. 

. . .

On Sunday night, he runs `git add .` and `git commit -m "fixed project stuff"`, 
pushing the entire thing to GitHub. 

. . .

On Monday morning, his professor points out that a code adjustment made on day 
4 accidentally ruined the data integrity pipeline. 

. . .

:::poll
Because Ryan mashed 21 days of complex, erratic file changes into a 
single history node, he cannot roll back the graph to isolate the error, 
forcing him to manually untangle his entire codebase.
:::


## 10. The "Free Real Estate" Licensing Illusion

. . .

An open-source research team discovers a student's public repository 
containing a clever, highly optimized data parsing code. 

. . .

They want to integrate it into a medical framework that could save lives, 
but their legal compliance department blocks it completely. 

. . .

Because the student forgot to include an explicit `LICENSE` file 
(like MIT or Apache 2.0), the code legally defaults to strict, 
restrictive copyright ownership. 

. . .

:::poll
The useful pipeline remains legally locked away from helping the community.
:::


# What is this class about {.nostretch}

## 

\

. . .

::: {.bigadage}
Simply put, this class is about learning tools and acquiring good practices to avoid those horror stories.
:::


## Reproducibility {auto-animate="true"}

. . .

::: {.poll}
A minimal standard for data analysis and other scientific computations 
is that they be [reproducible]{.bold-hilit}. 
:::


## Reproducibility {auto-animate="true"}

::: {.poll}
A minimal standard for data analysis and other scientific computations 
is that they be [reproducible]{.bold-hilit}. 

\

This means that the code and data are assembled in 
a way so that [another group]{.mdlit} can re-create all of the results 
(e.g., the figures in a paper).
:::

\

. . .

["another group"]{.mdlit} includes your future-self!


## Reproducibility

- Are the tables and figures reproducible from the code
and data?

- Does the code actually do what you think it does?

- In addition to what was done, is it clear why it was done?
    + (e.g., how were parameter settings chosen?)

- Can the code be used for other data?

- Can you extend the code to do other things?


## Basic Principles

- Everything via code

- Everything automated
    + Workflow and dependencies clearly documented

- Get the data in the most-raw form possible

- Get any/all data and meta-data possible

- Keep track of the provenance of all data files

- Be self-sufficient

- Determine what others can do with your code and media


## Why bother?

- Avoid embarrassment

- More likely correct

- Save time, in the long run

- Greater potential for extensions

- Higher impact

- Peace of mind


## Basic Tools

- Unix command line

- Version control with git

- Automation with Make

- Environment Management (e.g. Conda)

- Packages

- Dynamic Documents (notebooks, markdown)

- Website Compendiums (e.g. Quarto, MyST)


## Other Related Topics

- Organizing Projects

- Writing clear code

- Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

- Testing and debugging

- Handling data

- Producing figures

- Choosing Licenses

- Human subjects data (privacy)

## Parting words {auto-animate="true"}

::: {.poll}
Organizing analyses so that they are reproducible is not easy. 

\

It requires diligence and a considerable investment of time: 
to learn new computational tools, and to organize and document analyses as you go.

\

However, adopting a workflow that will make your results reproducible will 
ultimately make your life easier.
:::
